incidents.tldrRootCause: An employee's corporate GitHub account was taken over, likely via a stolen credential or token, and used to deploy malicious code.

incidents.howItCouldHitYou: If one of your GitHub accounts or tokens is taken over, and a single account can merge and deploy, an attacker can ship malicious code into your cloud backend the same way.
lockItDown: In GitHub rulesets or branch protection for branches that deploy to production, confirm pull request approval by another person is required and that admins cannot bypass it.

sources.name: BleepingComputer
sources.title: Remus malware steals Gmail messages via fake Google Sheets extension

incidents.title: Remus infostealer reads Gmail through a fake Google Sheets Chrome extension
incidents.evidenceQuote: stealing Gmail messages through a stealthy malicious Chrome extension
incidents.tldrRootCause: An infostealer installs a malicious Chrome extension posing as Google Sheets, which then reads Gmail messages from the logged-in browser.
incidents.realisticRootCause: The Remus infostealer uses a malicious Chrome extension to read Gmail from inside the browser session. Its operators marketed this as a Gmail zero-day, but the evidence describes an extension, not a flaw in Gmail; how Remus first lands on the machine is not stated.
incidents.couldThisHappenToMe: Yes, if an infostealer runs on a laptop where Chrome is signed in to Gmail; look for a Google Sheets extension nobody installed.
incidents.howItCouldHitYou: An infected Mac or Windows laptop gets a rogue extension added to Chrome, which reads mail (including password resets and cloud alerts) from the active session.
lockItDown: Open chrome://extensions on your laptops and remove anything you did not install, especially an extension named like Google Sheets that did not come from your own install.
If you manage Chrome centrally, check in the admin console's extension policy that installs are limited to an allowlist rather than open to any extension.
incidents.roleAngle: Session-level theft via an extension sidesteps MFA, so extension allowlisting is an identity control as much as an endpoint one.

lockItDown: Review the help desk procedure for password and MFA resets and confirm it requires verification that a caller cannot talk their way through, such as a callback to a number on record or manager approval.

incidents.roleAngle: The control gap is the reset process, not the MFA technology; a phishing-resistant factor helps little if a phone call can re-enrol it.

sources.name: GitHub Critical Advisories
sources.title: GHSA Critical (npm:ruflo): ruflo MCP bridge allows unauthenticated remote code execution in default Docker Compose deployments

incidents.title: ruflo MCP bridge: unauthenticated remote code execution in default Docker Compose setups
incidents.evidenceQuote: exposed POST /mcp with no authentication
incidents.attackSurface: Local AI dev tools / MCP server
incidents.tldrRootCause: The default compose file exposed the MCP endpoint without authentication and bound it and MongoDB to all network interfaces.
incidents.realisticRootCause: A network attacker could call terminal_execute through POST /mcp, get a shell in the bridge container and read every AI provider API key from its environment. They could also store poisoned patterns in the AgentDB learning store, which a patched redeploy does not remove. The advisory describes a flaw and does not report exploitation.
incidents.couldThisHappenToMe: Only if you or your developers run ruflo from its docker-compose.yml; look for listeners on ports 3001 and 27017.
incidents.howItCouldHitYou: A ruflo instance started with the default compose file on a laptop or cloud VM would be reachable by anyone on the same network, or the internet, exposing AI provider keys.
lockItDown: Check whether ruflo is deployed anywhere, and if so that ports 3001 and 27017 are bound to loopback or firewalled, and that it runs the fixed version with MCP_AUTH_TOKEN set.
If an instance was ever exposed, rotate the OpenAI, Google, OpenRouter and Anthropic keys in its environment and audit the AgentDB pattern store for injected entries.
incidents.roleAngle: A clear example of agent tooling shipping with bind-all, no-auth defaults; worth checking other MCP servers your developers run for the same pattern.

sources.title: SYS010 malware abuses browser management to spy on Gmail, Outlook

incidents.title: SYS01 infostealer enrols browsers in management to force a mail-stealing extension
incidents.evidenceQuote: SYS01 infostealer malware delivered through Meta ads is enrolling browsers into enterprise-style management
incidents.tldrRootCause: Users are lured by Meta ads into running the SYS01 infostealer, which enrols the browser in management and force-installs an extension.
incidents.realisticRootCause: A new SYS01 version sets enterprise-style browser management on the victim's machine so it can force-install an extension. That extension steals sensitive data, including Gmail and Outlook emails.
incidents.couldThisHappenToMe: Yes, if someone on a Mac or Windows laptop runs a download from a malicious Meta ad; unmanaged personal browsers are the most exposed.
incidents.howItCouldHitYou: A lure from an ad leads to malware on a laptop, which then controls the browser by policy and reads webmail sessions, including any used for work.
lockItDown: Open chrome://management (or edge://management) and confirm the browser is managed only by your own organization, or not at all on personal devices.
Open chrome://policy and look for force-installed extension entries (ExtensionInstallForcelist) you do not recognise.
incidents.roleAngle: Browser policy is now a persistence mechanism; unexpected 'managed by your organization' banners on unmanaged devices are a detection signal.

If either is present, treat the machine as potentially compromised until checked against the researchers' published indicators, and re-issue credentials and sessions used on it.

sources.name: The Hacker News
sources.title: North Korea-Linked PolinRider Poisons Over 7,600 GitHub Repositories to Spread Malware

incidents.title: PolinRider campaign compromises over 7,600 GitHub repositories owned by real developers
incidents.tldrRootCause: Not disclosed: how the developers' accounts or repos were taken over is not in the excerpt, only that real repos were poisoned with a Python loader.
incidents.realisticRootCause: Not disclosed in the evidence. Apiiro reports that over 7,600 repositories were compromised, most belonging to real developers rather than throwaway accounts. incidents.couldThisHappenToMe: Possibly: your own GitHub repos could be poisoned the same way, or you could clone and run code from a repo that already has been.

lockItDown: Review your GitHub security log, plus personal access tokens, SSH keys and authorized OAuth apps in account settings, for anything you do not recognise.
Check recent commit history on your repos and on third-party repos you build from for unexpected commits adding or changing Python files.
incidents.roleAngle: A repo owned by a legitimate, long-standing developer account is not evidence that its latest commit is trustworthy.

sources.name: The Hacker News
sources.title: Okta Links ShinyHunters-Associated Vishing Group to New INCEPTION Data Leak Site

incidents.title: Okta links ShinyHunters-associated vishing cluster O-UNC-053 to new INCEPTION leak site
incidents.evidenceQuote: use of voice phishing (aka vishing) attacks to trick targets into entering credentials in phishing pages
incidents.tldrRootCause: Callers talk targets into entering their credentials on phishing pages and then approving something; the excerpt is cut off before saying what.
incidents.realisticRootCause: Okta's Threat Intelligence team says the cluster uses voice calls to steer targets to credential phishing pages and then to approve a further step. It assesses that the group may have rebranded as INCEPTION and now runs a data leak site.
incidents.couldThisHappenToMe: Yes: anyone signing in through SSO with a password plus an approval-based second factor can be talked through this by phone.
incidents.howItCouldHitYou: A caller posing as IT support could walk you or a colleague through a fake SSO page, gaining a session that reaches the cloud consoles, GitHub and SaaS behind it.
lockItDown: In your identity provider's authentication policies, check whether admin and cloud console sign-ins still accept push, SMS or OTP rather than only FIDO2 or passkeys.
Review identity provider logs for recent new authenticator or device enrolments that the account owner cannot confirm.
incidents.roleAngle: Phishing-resistant authenticators are the control that defeats this pattern, because user awareness fails under a convincing live call.

sources.name: The Hacker News
sources.title: Researchers Demonstrate Ghostscript Sandbox-Escape RCE via Crafted File Uploads in Popular Apps

incidents.title: Ghostscript sandbox-escape RCE shown via crafted file uploads; patch available
incidents.evidenceQuote: allows a crafted file to escape the program's security sandbox and run commands on the server that processes it
incidents.attackSurface: File upload / document conversion on Linux servers and containers
incidents.tldrRootCause: A crafted uploaded file escapes Ghostscript's sandbox and runs commands on the server that converts it.
incidents.realisticRootCause: A now-patched Ghostscript flaw lets a malicious PDF, PostScript or image file break out of the interpreter's sandbox. Ghostscript is often invoked indirectly by other software during upload conversion, so applications can be exposed without calling it themselves. The evidence describes a researcher demonstration, not in-the-wild exploitation.
incidents.couldThisHappenToMe: Yes, if any of your cloud workloads or container images include Ghostscript and process user-uploaded PDFs, PostScript or images.
incidents.howItCouldHitYou: A Linux container or VM in your cloud that generates thumbnails or converts uploaded documents may pull in Ghostscript as a dependency, giving an uploader command execution on that workload.
lockItDown: Search your container image and host package inventories (SBOM or vulnerability scanner results) for the ghostscript package and confirm it is at the patched version from your distribution.
Identify services that accept file uploads and convert or preview them, and check whether that conversion runs in an isolated, low-privilege workload without cloud credentials it does not need.
incidents.roleAngle: Indirect dependencies in image-processing pipelines are an easy-to-miss route to code execution in cloud workloads.

sources.name: BleepingComputer
sources.title: New NFS2ROOT Linux flaw can let attackers gain root privileges

incidents.title: NFS2ROOT: 12-year-old Linux kernel NFS server flaw allows remote root (CVE-2026-99362)
incidents.evidenceQuote: allows remote attackers to gain root privileges
incidents.attackSurface: Linux kernel NFS server on cloud hosts and nodes
incidents.tldrRootCause: A critical flaw in the Linux kernel's NFS server lets a remote attacker gain root; the evidence does not report exploitation in the wild.
incidents.realisticRootCause: CVE-2026-99362 is in the kernel's Network File System server and has been present for about 12 years. The teaser gives no affected versions, required configuration or patch status.
incidents.couldThisHappenToMe: Possibly: look for Linux VMs or Kubernetes nodes that run the kernel NFS server (nfsd) and are reachable on the NFS port.
incidents.howItCouldHitYou: A self-managed Linux host exporting NFS in your cloud accounts, reachable by an attacker over the network, could be taken over as root and used to pivot into workloads and their credentials.
lockItDown: Review security groups and firewall rules in AWS, GCP and Azure for inbound TCP 2049 (NFS) allowed from wide ranges, and restrict it to known clients.
Inventory Linux VMs and Kubernetes nodes that run the kernel NFS server, and schedule the distribution's kernel update for them once it is available.
incidents.roleAngle: Self-managed NFS exports on cloud VMs are often forgotten; this is a reason to find them.

sources.name: Google Project Zero
sources.title: VirtualBox Process Hardening on Windows 2026 Edition: What’s a Single Bit Between Friends?

incidents.title: Project Zero: .NET loading quirk bypasses VirtualBox hardening and Windows code integrity
incidents.evidenceQuote: permitted a bypass of the checks and allowed me to load arbitrary code into the protected process
incidents.tldrRootCause: A .NET Framework assembly-loading behaviour combined with VirtualBox's DLL loader hooks let a local attacker load arbitrary code into a protected process.
incidents.realisticRootCause: This is researcher-demonstrated, with no exploitation in the wild reported. CVE-2026-87268 abuses .NET's ability to load assemblies from memory to get past VirtualBox process hardening on Windows hosts; the same behaviour bypassed Windows code integrity. It requires an attacker already running code locally.
incidents.couldThisHappenToMe: Only on Windows laptops, and mainly if Oracle VirtualBox is installed; it needs an attacker who already has local code execution.
incidents.howItCouldHitYou: Malware already running as a user on a Windows laptop with VirtualBox could use this to load code into a protected process and potentially escalate privileges.
lockItDown: Check Windows laptops for Oracle VirtualBox under Settings > Apps > Installed apps; update it to the latest release or remove it if unused.
Confirm Windows Update is current on those machines, since the write-up also covers a Windows code integrity bypass.
incidents.roleAngle: Developer laptops often carry old virtualisation tools with kernel drivers; these are a common local privilege escalation route.

lockItDown: In GitHub organisation settings, confirm secret scanning and push protection are enabled for all repositories, and review any open secret scanning alerts.
Review Microsoft's post for the ARTEX network and system activity indicators and hunting queries, and check them against your logs.
incidents.roleAngle: Automation shortens the time between a secret being exposed in a public repository and it being used.

incidents.title: Reporter with no experience uses free AI models to find WordPress plugin CSRF in six hours
incidents.tldrRootCause: Not an incident: a first-person account of finding and reporting a CSRF bug in a WordPress plugin with help from two free LLMs.
incidents.realisticRootCause: The author found, tested and reported a cross-site request forgery in a plugin with over 40,000 active installations, assigned CVE-2026-124251. The excerpt does not name the plugin and describes no exploitation.
incidents.couldThisHappenToMe: No direct exposure: WordPress is not in your footprint and the plugin is not named in the evidence.
incidents.howItCouldHitYou: There is no direct path; the relevance is the trend that people with little experience can now find real bugs with AI help.
incidents.roleAngle: Useful talking point: the skill barrier for finding common bug classes is dropping, so expect more reports and more low-effort discovery against your own code.

incidents.title: WhatsApp patches three flaws, including an Android ad-reply URL bug possibly used in scams
incidents.evidenceQuote: incomplete validation of external ad-reply URLs in WhatsApp for Android and WhatsApp Business for Android before 2.26.17.4
incidents.tldrRootCause: WhatsApp for Android did not fully validate external ad-reply URLs; Meta suspects this was abused in scam messages.
incidents.realisticRootCause: CVE-2026-23871 (CVSS 3.5) affects WhatsApp and WhatsApp Business for Android before 2.26.17.4. Exploitation is suspected, not confirmed, and is linked to scam messages.
incidents.couldThisHappenToMe: Not through your work footprint; it only matters if you use WhatsApp on an Android phone older than version 2.26.17.4.
incidents.howItCouldHitYou: There is no path to cloud, GitHub, SSO or laptops; this is a low-severity mobile app bug.
